sources.name: IGFA world record search: Eel, American (all-tackle 4.21 kg, Cape May, New Jersey, 1995)
Chesapeake Bay Program field guide: American eel
Florida freshwater regulations (FWC guide): bag and length limits (American eel)

lengthWeight.source: FishBase LWR table: Altamaha River, Georgia (spring sample), TL, mixed sexes

growth.source: FishBase growth table: Nova Scotia, TL (no southern entries). Max age FishBase; South Carolina DNR notes southern eels live much shorter lives (about 9 years for females, 5 for males).

size.notes: FishBase gives a 152 cm TL maximum and a 7.3 kg maximum weight, but the angling record is 4.21 kg; lengthCm.max set to 131 cm, where the Georgia LWR meets the IGFA record. Only females grow large (males to about 60 cm).

spawn.notes: Adults leave in October for the Sargasso Sea, spawn in January and die. Spawning has never been observed. Off the map: no in-game spawning.

migration.notes: Mature silver eels run downstream and out to sea in autumn; glass eels and elvers enter rivers in late winter and spring and move upstream in large numbers (Chesapeake Bay Program, SC DNR).

markings.where: edges of the dorsal and anal fins

pattern.fins: one continuous fin fringe from mid-back around the tail to the vent; no pelvic fins; small rounded pectorals; lower jaw longer than the upper; thick lips

variants.juvenile: glass eel: transparent; elver: brown, about 6 cm; yellow eel: greenish, yellowish-brown or blackish above, whitish below
variants.spawning_migrant: silver eel: sexually mature adults turn silver for the run to sea

pattern.source: Chesapeake Bay Program field guide; South Carolina DNR; FishBase short description

regulations.notes: Fresh water: 25 eels a day, each at least 9 in total length (bought bait eels exempt). Listed Endangered by IUCN: release is rewarded.

economy.notes: A delicacy in Europe and Asia; most eels caught in the US are exported.

facts: Every American eel is born in the Sargasso Sea; adults leave the rivers in October, spawn there in January and die.
Eels can slither over rocks, dams and wet grass to get upstream.
The species is listed as Endangered by the IUCN.

research.task: Catch one on a nightcrawler on the bottom at night
Observe elvers moving upstream in spring

ledger.wrenNote: An eel will tie your line in knots if you give him slack. Keep him coming steady, don't let him back into the rocks, and don't grab him bare-handed. Wet rag, or straight into the bucket.
